Mr. FOSTER

I promised the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket) yesterday, that I would look into the question raised by him in reference to an answer to a question, on the order paper, of the hon. the Minister of Public Works. The answer referred to stated that a certain company declined to tender for certain work and that the said company gave as a reason for declining that they found certain difficulties attending upon the work. The hon. member for York asked the hon. minister to lay the papers referred to on the table. As a matter of fact, the answer of the hon. minister did not refer to any papers, and the hon. minister himself stated to the House that he was not sure there was any correspondence on the subject. The hon. member for York asked if he was not entitled to demand that the correspondence, if anyj be laid upon the table without an order of the House.	-
The rule of parliament in respect to the production of papers is that no documents can be laid before the House unless in pursuance of some parliamentary authority. The proper parliamentary authority is, of course, an order of the House, which must be moved for under the rules of the House as to notice. There is, however, a rule of debate, which the hon. member for York probably had in his mind, to the effect that when a minister of the Crown quotes a public document in the House and founds upon it an argument or assertion, the document quoted from should be produced. This rule does not apply to the case in question, as I do not find that the hon. minister quoted from any public document; in fact, he stated that he was not sure there was any correspondence on the subject. I am of opinion, therefore, that the hon. member for York is not entitled to the production of any correspondence or papers, if any, without following the rule of the House as to papers, on motion after notice.

Hon. SYDNEY FISHER-for Hon. W. S. Fielding-moved that the House go into committee on Tuesday next to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide for a revision and amendment of the Currency Act, chapter 25, of the Revised Statutes.
Further resolved, that the standard for gold coins of the currency of Canada be such that of one thousand parts by weight, nine hundred shall be of fine gold and one hundred of alloy; and the standard for silver coin shall be such that of one thousand parts by weight nine hundred and twenty-five shall be of fine silver and seventy-five of alloy ; that the

standard weight for gold coin of the denomination of ten dollars in the currency of Canada he two hundred and fifty-eight grains, and the standard weight for a silver coin of the denomination of fifty cents be one hundred and eighty grains, and for other gold coins and silver coins proportionate weights respectively; that the Minister of Finance be authorized to issue out of the consolidated revenue fund such sums as may be necessary for the purchase of bullion in order to provide supplies of coins for the public service; and that the cost, charges and expenses incident to carrying out the provisions of any Act founded upon these resolutions be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.
Motion agreed to.

I would ask the attention of the Minister of Railways to a return ordered on December 1, as to passes on the Intercolonial railway. That motion includes another for the production of the papers in reference to the purchase of ties on the Windsor branch. If the former papers could be brought down the later papers might remain for the present. COMMON ri

A similar return was asked this year and we are trying to complete what was brought down last year, making an addition to it. If I remember correctly, the commissioners said last year that it was impossible to give those particulars.
I think they can give them if they wish.

I wish to draw the attention of the government to an article which appears in the New York ' Herald ' of yesterday. The title of which is ' Dominion government refuses to' accept German concession for the removal of the surtax.' I wish to ask the government whether it is true that they have received a communication from the German government in regard to the removal of the surtax and whether they have decided to take any action in the matter. The article goes on to say that Italy and Belgium, both of whom will be hurt by the Franco-Canadian treaty which goes into effect January 1, are pressing the government for as favourable concessions as France secures and are prepared to retaliate if they are not accorded. I would ask the government whether Italy and Belgium have also pressed on thq government the necessity for better trade relations and whether they have been refused in the same manner as, according to this article, Germany ha3 been. This is an important article, we have the privilege of having a member in the press gallery who represents this paper and whose presence, I am sure, we all appreciate and if the Prime Minister will be good enough to answer those two questions I would appreciate it.

I asked whether Mr. Allard had been connected with the government contracts directly or indirectly on January 22. Of course he might have been interested last Saturday and not yesterday. I would like my right hon. friend to answer the question as it is worded, if he is prepared to do so. I Mr. FOSTER.
would like to have the answer a little more definite if possible. Was he interested on January 22 and has the Prime Minister sufficient information to enable him to say unequivocally that he had not on that day any such interest.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no information whatever. It is quite possible, I do not know, that Mr. Allard or any body else may have had contracts with different branches of the government, but it would take some time for the government to find out. Mr. FISHER moved the second Teading of Bill (No. 55) to amend the Seed Control Act.
Has there been an explanation of this Bill?

Yes, I explained the Bill on its introduction. But, should an explanation be desired now, I may say that, in the course of the operation of the Seed Control Act, some slight difficulties-very few, I am 84*
happy to say-have arisen, and this Bill is intended to obviate those difficulties. In addition, the Bill adopts a new principle in seed control. Hitherto we have dealt only with the purity of seeds; now we propose to deal with the vitality of seeds. The clauses relating to purity have helped to protect the farmers against the purchase of weed seeds or of seeds of a different variety from that which they desire to purchase. Now it is proposed to protect the farmers-from having seed palmed off on them the percentage of whose vitality is not up to a fair standard. This has not been embodied, in the Act heretofore, but we have found; in some instances that the loss of the farmers in consequence of this inferior quality of the seed has been very considerable, and we wish to take the necessary means to protect them. The first clause of the Bill simply authorizes the making of regulations for this purpose, and the last clause provides that labels on packages of seeds must state the percentage capable of germination. The third section brings under the operation of the Act alfalfa, now a very important farm crop, to be dealt with as grass and clover seeds have been dealt with heretofore. The Bill also adds wild radish to the list of prohibited seeds and introduces some explanatory names of seeds mentioned in the seventh section of the Act.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon.
On section 1,
1. Subsection 1 of section 2 of the Seed Control Act, chapter 128, of the Revised Statutes, 1906, is amended by adding the following paragraph immediately after paragrapn (u.) tnere-of:-
(aa) regulations determining the percentage standards of vitality for good seed of the various kinds of cereals, grasses, clovers, forage plants, field root and garden vegetaolo crops; and,

I have just explained that section 2 of the Act as- it stands authorizes the making of regulations determining the maximum proportion of the seed of weeds named in the Act that may be tolerated in other seeds, and also such regulations as are necessary to secure the due enforcement of the Act. Under this proposed section, we shall also make regulations to provide standards of vitality.
Would the minister -be good enough to give us some idea of what success is being met with in carrying out the Act.

I am not sure that that is a subject I should take up on thi3 section, but, as I wish to give all the information possible, I will say in general terms that it has been very successful in improving the

quality of seeds supplied to our farmers. In the first place, it has attracted the attention of farmers to the quality of the seed, and, in the second place, has required seed merchants and sellers throughout the country to live up to the law. And, with their desire to do so-which I may say is general-they have the knowledge that if they do not do so they are called to account. This is not always by prosecution necessarily, although a number of prosecutions have been entered. We try wherever possible, where apparently the dereliction of duty has not- been intentional, to admonish rather than punish. But where the lack of proper supervision is apparently due, either tc gross carelessness or deliberate intention, we do not hesitate to put the Act into force. I am glad to say that even in respect of those who have violated the Act, the course we have adopted, and the existence of the Act itself, have tended greatly to raise the quality of the seeds supplied to our farmers. I am also glad to say that the farmers who buy seeds, knowing of the existence of this Act and of the machinery which is provided to enable them to get good seeds, are firstly, paying more attention to the quality and character of their seeds, and secondly, are taking the trouble to send samples to the laboratory here, where they are tested, and where information is given to the farmers of the character of the seeds which they are purchasing.

The reason I ask the question is that I understand there are quite a number of farmers, who take advantage of the privilege of sending their seeds here to be tested, but nothing like the extent that the minister would perhaps lead us to believe. Do the farmers generally know that this Act is in existence, and do they take the trouble to purchase pure seeds from the local dealer, or are they allowed, as the old Act, if I remember rightly, gave them the privilege, to dispose of their seed to the retail man, and the retail man, instead of buying from the wholesaler, is buying from the farmers? Then, would the minister be good enough to tell us about how many inspectors he has looking after the Seeds Mark Act, and about how many prosecutions there are per annum?

There are seven inspectors whose special business it is, in that period of the year when seeds are bought and sold, to look after this business, and they take samples amongst those who are selling seeds. The Act empowers them to go in and buy a sample and make a test of it for themselves, without the intervention of the purchaser or the farmer. At the same time, the farmer can also send samples to be tested. The seed men themselves frequently send samples; nearly half the seeds that are tested here come from Mr. FISHER
the. seed sellers. They desire that the seeds they are selling should be up to the standard of the Act, showing, as I have already said, their desire to do what is right. The machinery of the department in the seed laboratory is a great assistance to them; without it, each of them would have to have a testing machinery of his own, which would be almost impossible for them to get. We have a staff of experts here who have been trained in that work for a long time, and who are able to do it. Some of the large seed houses do this for themselves, but the smaller ones and the retailers do noL In this way we are fully aware of the improvement that has been made, and that improvement is far greater than the number of prosecutions undertaken, whether successful or not, would indicate.

I have been conversing with some of the western men, and I find, as the minister may be well aware, that hundreds and thousands of acres of grain are burned every year, for instance, in the province of Manitoba, by the weed inspector. Of course the land has a good deal to do with that, the land has been permeated to a certain extent with these seeds. Does the minister mean to say that farmers in general throughout the northwest, as well as eastern provinces, are conversant to any extent with the clauses in the Seeds Marks Act? I cannot help but think that they are not in touch with the operation of the Act to a large extent, or they are paying very little attention to it.

The power to burn up foul seeds in the field is taken under a provincial law and not under this Act. I regret that the fields of the west, as well as the fields of the eastern part of Canada, are very foul. It is very regrettable, and one of the chief objects of the Seeds Commissioners branch is to try and assist the farmers to improve that condition of things. But it is a slow process, it can only be carried out with the co-operation of the owners of the land themselves. All we can do in that regard is to urge upon them the necessity of improvement, and to suggest methods by which they can effect an improvement, and save the vast loss which is entailed upon them year by year by neglecting to clean their land. As to the knowledge of the farmers of this Act, I think it is pretty widespread. My hon. friend will remember that two years ago, about the time this Act was passed, we sent through the northwest a special train carrying samples of seeds and grains, and a staff of expert officers. They held about 200 meetings in the three prairie provinces, mostly in Manitoba and Sask-

atchewan. They were very largely advertised, and commented upon, and discussed, even by those who were not able to attend the meetings. It was a very graphic and effective way of calling the attention of the public to this evil, and to methods of remedy. Since that time we have had, with the co-operation of the seed growers, local associations, or branches established, and a very large number of meetings have been held, dealing almost entirely with the question of the purity of the seeds. In addition to that, the various institute meetings in the several provinces, this question has been frequently discussed, and the farmers have taken a great interest in it. I may say that the grain farmers, especially of the west, have been thoroughly aroused to the necessity of action. I grant that a great many of the farmers of Canada, perhaps the larger number, do not carry out the advice that is given to them. It is perhaps too much to expect at present, although we think that they will do more. Farmers are like the rest of us, they probably do not do quite as well as they know how. There are hundreds and thousands of farmers in Canada who have been made acquainted with the information supplied by the department on this subject, they are advised to do certain things to clean their land, and yet many of them, for lack of time or energy, fail to act upon our advice. We can only hope that as time goes on our farmers will more generally take advantage of the machinery provided in the Act, and I think we are gradually overcoming the apathy which has existed.

I cannot help feeling that altogether a more aggressive policy ought to * be adopted in the eastern provinces in carrying out the policy of the government in this regard. When you take into consideration there are 23,000,000 acres under crop, if you could increase the production by a bushel or two per acre per annum, see the millions of dollars it would bring back to the farmers. If merely a few copies of this Act, or the instructions go out to a small number of farmers it is not likely that the aggressive policy is being pursued that should be carried on. I think it would be well if the minister could devise some means whereby he could undertake a more aggressive policy upon this subject.

When this movement began the government sent a car through our part of the country to show the advantages of the use of pure seed. But, unfortunately, that policy of the government, has not as far as I know been continued, and nothing further has been done in that direction. I do not think there Is
one man in a thousand among merchants or farmers, or the men who handle seed grain, in our part of the country, who knows anything about the Pure Seed Act. It is a very important question. Our western country is subject to foul seeds of every kind. They grow very luxuriantly and very rapidly. They seem to take the place of almost any useful crop. That is one of the evils that we will have to contend with in that country, and I think the government should continue the propaganda and the policy of distributing more information in that direction.
Do I understand my hon. friend to say that we are doing nothing in the neighbourhood in which he lives?

I do not believe that one man in a thousand knows anything in particular about your pure seed Bill. I do not think that very much has been done in the last two or three years in the direction of educating the farmers.

Well, we have regularly, for several years, conducted field crop competitions in the hon. gentleman's own constituency, and there were thirteen seed fairs held last year in Alberta for the special purpose of explaining to the farmers the advantages of good seed and of getting them to buy good seed. I think I am within the mark when I say that from 40,000 to 50,000 copies of our special seed bulletins and the Seed Act have been distributed each year by my department. I think that my hon. friend a little underrates the intelligence and knowledge of his own people. He will find- that a good many of his farmers know about this, about these seed fairs, about the field crop competitions and about the work of the seed growers associations which are working locally, as our department is working for the whole country. We are aiding and co-operating with these associations, stimulating and helping them on. I sympathize with the feelings of the hon. gentleman when he says that enough is not being done, but at the same time, I have learned by long experience that you have to exercise some patience before seeing plainly the results of work of this kind which is done in agriculture. You do not get the results all at once. The spread of information, the improvement of methods, and all that is very slow and it is especially a case where, in our western country, a great many of the men who own and work the land were not brought up as farmers.	It is a great deal
harder to teach these people than it is to teach young men who have grown up with and been accustome 1 to agricultural work from their childhood,

and especially people who have come from abroad and who are not familiar with our conditions. I am just as eager as any one to do all that can be done profitably and advantageously, and I must confess to my hon. friend that nearly every year I am asking for a little more money to expend in this way. But I would like to have a thorough scheme of organization and of work to ensure that the money spent will give a good return. I do not want to ask parliament for money to spend uselessly for the purpose of making a show of spending money and of being able to say that so much money has been spent. I have never done that in connection *with any of the work of my department, and I do not like to do it now. If any suggestion is made, and occasionally I get valuable suggestions from members of the House, farmers, and leading men of the country, I am only too happy to take it up and see whether it will work into practical organization or operation for the benefit of the farmers. I think we have done that about as much as we could. We are doing a a great deal of work at the present time in connection with the improvement of iseed. My seed commissioner gives his whole time to it and we have the further satisfaction of knowing that other countries, notably the United States, are looking to us and to this very Seed Control Act for models upon which to base their legislation and work.
The minister stated that several seed fairs have been held.
Thirteen in the province of Alberta.
Were they in my constituency?
No; I said thirteen in the province of Alberta, but I also said 'that there were field crop competitions held in the hon. gentleman's own county. That is another thing.
Where would they be in my own constituency?
The Fishburn Agricul-, tural Society has been co-operating with the department and carrying on that work.

I am very glad to hear it, but I would like to say a further word in reference to this seed train that passed through our country a few years ago exhibiting pure seed. I think that it gave a splendid education to the farmers and did a great deal of good to the country. I am sorry that something of the kind could not be undertaken again. I believe that is one of the best ways of educating the farmers that I have ever seen, and from that day to the present I have not Mr. FISHER.
seen anything that has impressed me as being of such value in that direction. It may have been costly, but I think it was of great value to the country.

I quite agree with .my hon. friend that such a work as that seed train did is very effective. In waking up the people to a certain line of work we find, first, that we have to do something that is very striking, something that will attract public attention, something that will awaken and arouse them, and then we have to take it up more in detail by instructive and helpful co-operation with the people individually. The results of that are not as conspicuous and a great deal of the work is being done silently without its attracting the interest or observation of the people at large. But it is just as necessary to go through that second stage or phase of the work as it is to do the more conspicuous! *or the more brilliant work at the commencement. I can assure my hon. friend that while we have not been doing anything quite so brilliant as that train, we have been doing just as effective work in' the present stage of the education of the people. I am not afraid of the expense, and if it is necessary to arouse the people again to do something of that kind, I would not hesitate because it costs money, and I am sure, judging from experience, that parliament will foe good enough to grant me the necessary funds. I am glad the suggestion has been made as to whether we should not repeat the experiment.

Did the hon. gentleman have any co-operation between the government and the provincial authorities or between the government and the railway companies, or did he simply engage in this enterprise alone? In the United States the railways would seem to be very generous in the contribution of car facilities, and of course it is to their advantage because every good bushel of grain, instead of a bad bushel, brings them more trade. It is just as much the duty of the up to date provincial agricultural authorities as it is ours that such work should be done, and co-operation would make the work more effective and more economical.
The provincial authorities were invited to co-operate, and the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan did. The railways supplied the rolling stock and hauled the train free.

I sympathize with all reasonable efforts to prevent the spreading of foul seeds, but I think this Act provides for a penalty on the man who sells foul seed whether he has knowledge that the seed is foul or not. That may prove to be, rather harsh. For instance, a farmer might not know there was foul seed in the clover
seed he sells and it would be going very far to impose a penalty on him.

If I require to show every time a prosecution is entered that the person selling impure seed knew he was doing so, I would practically have to give up all attempt to enforce the Act. If persons offer for sale seed as pure, it should ba pure, and we must trust to them taking the necessary precautions.
I do not think a penalty should he imposed unless the man had knowledge he was selling impure seed.
I take direct issue with my hon. friend there.
Surely guilty knowledge must he the essence of an offence of that sort.

If a man engaged in business sells me seed as pure, it is his business to know. In subsection 2 of section 9 if the man can prove he bought the seed in good faith from a wholesale merchant, the onus is thrown on the wholesale merchant.
But suppose the man grew the seed?
Then he would have to take the consequences.
I think that would be harsh treatment.

There has been a good deal done by the provincial and Dominion governments to prevent the distribution of wild seeds through the sale of seed grain and grass and clover seeds, but there is another mode of distributing these wild seeds to which I would direct attention. The milling companies grind their screenings, but they do not grind them fine enough in some cases, and the most dangerous weeds in the section of the country I live in, as well as in other parts pf Ontario, have been introduced through the importation of ground feed. We have no knowledge in the world when we buy that feed that we are going to pollute our farms, but nevertheless' that has been the result. While the distribution of wild seeds is met in the Bill in some aspects, something should be done to take precautions in the direction I have mentioned.

That is a pretty difficult problem to deal with. The provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba have provincial statutes which cover that point, and which if they are enforced would seem to be calculated to meet the difficulty pretty successfully. I do not think the province of Ontario has any such law, or, if so, it is entirely obsolete. The situation, is a little different in the different provinces, and their laws have practically to
be different. I am advised that it would be extremelv difficult, if not impossible, for us to draw a general law applicable to the whole Dominion which would cover the ground as well as the provincial laws. In each of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta there is a provincial law on the subject. This question has been considered pretty carefully by us, but there is nothing in this Act which deals with that.

I am well aware that noxious seeds exported from the west have been distributed through the province of Ontario, especially in the vicinity where I live. I am glad to learn that the western provinces have laws to prevent this; but during the last five years I myself have received the seeds of foul plants that have never existed in our part of the country before, through the buying of western feed, many of the farmers in Ontario have come to the conclusion that it would be better to buy no western feed at all than to take the chances of polluting their farms with these noxious plants.

I sympathize with my hon. friend on that point. I believe the tailings of screenings that come from the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur are the principal media for the distribution of these foul weeds. These tailings or screenings are bought by the millers of Ontario, mixed with other grains, ground, and sold as feed, but they are not ground sufficiently fine to destroy all the weed seeds. It is a problem worthy of consideration whether something ought not to be done to restrain the distribution of these screenings. It is a matter which is under my consideration and which will have to be discussed in dealing with the terminal elevator question.

I do not see that there could be any objection to amending the Act to prevent the milling companies disposing of these screenings unless they are ground so fine that the seeds will not germinate, and to prevent them mixing them with other grains and selling the mixture as pure feed.

The farmers frequently prefer feed that is not ground too fine; and to grind these western tailings so fine as to kill some of the smallest seeds would be a pretty difficult process. I have had some investigation made into that question,- but perhaps not sufficient to make me very positive.
Perhaps it would be wise for the minister to make further investigation, and to compel the people grinding these screenings to sell them separately and not to mix them with other grains.

My experience is that the farmers are discarding the mills run with wind-power or horse-power because they do not grind fine enough, and are sending their grain to the large mills to get it ground finer. They believe that the finer the grain is ground, up to a certain standard, the better feed it is. My information in regard to this Seed Act is that while it provides for a certain standard of purity, and while the seedsmen generally comply with it and label their seeds No. 1, the Gomplaint is that you find, some months or a year after you have bought the seed, that you have introduced a lot of noxious weeds into your farm. For instance, you cannot buy turnip seed without getting with it a great deal of wild mustard, and the same thing is true of much of the clover seed that is sold. It is difficult to say what remedy could be applied to prevent this, but I know that there are a large number of complaints of that character.

If the farmers would purchase their seeds a little early and send a sample to be tested at the laboratory here they would get a reply in two or three weeks or perhaps less, and would know whether the seeds were what they had bought or not. It is hardly possible to tell the difference between mustard and turnip seed by the eye, but by testing them here they can easily be distinguished.
The trouble is the seed is usually brought in just before seeding time.
The farmer has the other remedy of buying only seed marked No. 1, which, from our experience with a large number of samples, almost invariably fulfils the condition of No. I.
What are you to do when you find they are not No. I?
We have found verv few samples of No. 1 that did not fulfil the conditions. I think the trouble is the farmers will not insist on buying No. 1.
From my experience and knowledge I am satisfied that in many cases they do not fulfil the conditions. On my own farm I have sowed seeds marked No. 1 that contained a great number of weeds.
I am sorry my hon. friend did not report that to the department. We have occasionally had reports sent, and we have traced them up. Even after the seeds are sown the purchaser is liable to a penalty.
You have difficulty in the enforcement of the Act when you have to go into court.
Keep a sample of the seed and send it to be tested.

Most farmers do not do that. When they sow No. 1 they do not retain a sample. I think that the common law should give damages in such a case, but owing to the difficulty of proving that the weeds came from the seed no farmer would go to the trouble of undertaking a prosecution. The Act is not as valuable in its working out to the farmers as they anticipated, because of these difficulties.
If a farmer will not take the trouble to protect himself, we cannot protect him. The farmer can test the seed before he sows it.
He cannot get it from the seedsman until a day or two before he wishes to use it.
As a rule he can get it earlier.
My office is right at a seed store, and I have seen the seed brought in hundreds of times after seeding was partly or principally over, even telegraph orders being sent to supply the demand.

Having failed to protect himself in that way, the farmer has the further protection of reserving a small package of seed, sufficient to make a test. When he has this proof, not only can he prosecute, but if he will let us know we will prosecute for him. We have had very few failures of prosecutions under this Act, and in many instances, without absolutely prosecuting, we have been able to change the whole current of the seed business in a locality by pointing out the truth in regard to the quality of these seeds. It is a physical inability, though, to protect people who will not protect themselves.
How many inspectors are there under this Act and what salaries do they receive?

I think seven altogether, and they are moving around the country. Some of them work in particular regions most of the time, and are backwards and forwards, but most of them are not located in any particular place.
How many of them are in the west?
Mr. Murray, of the Experimental Farm, Brandon; Mr. Eddy, Mr. Eeid and Mr. Mackillican.
Are they on the road all the time?

Just during the busy season. Mr. Murray gets his salary as manager of the Experimental Farm, and does

not get additional pay for seed inspection work. They are in a certain division of the Civil Service, subdivision 'A' of the second division. I could not give, offhand, the exact salary of each, but the salaries of that subdivision run from $1,600 to $2,100.
How many prosecutions have there been during last year throughout the Dominion?
Thirty-seven.

I appreciate the efforts of the minister (Mr. Fisher) to deal with this very important question. But there is a difficulty still existing that, it seems to me, is hard to get over. A farmer goes into a seed store and the merchant shows him perhaps half a dozen samples of seeds at different prices. And I have known instances where farmers are inclined to buy-like many other people-a cheap article. Taking that seed home and sowing it, of course, may be said to be the farmer's own business. But the difficulty is that he is sowing weed seeds, and his neighbour, no matter how cautious he may be with regard to the seed that goes into his own land, has to share in the difficulty that follows. The foul seed is apt to spread all over the locality. I do not think that any dealer should be allowed to put on the market a low grade of seed, even at a low price; such seed should not be put on the market at all. There should be a standard, and no seed should be allowed to be sold below that standard.
We have a standard below which no seed may be sold with a mark to indicate that it is No. 1. We have no definition of lower standards.
How do you make the grade?
No. I seed is described in the Act, and nothing below the standard there fixed can be sold as No. 1.
How do you make the test?

It has to be made in the laboratory. Of course, you cannot make it in a store. But if a man sells as No. 1 seed which is belo\f the standard here fixed, he is liable to a prosecution for a misdemeanour under the Act.
Is not that standard test made by actual count?-not more than so many weed seeds to be found in one hundred. With reference to the viability, that would be matter of growth, of course.
Section 7 fixes the standard, and provides that the seed must be free from the seeds of the weed named in the preceding section.
And that, as I understand, is determined by actual count. But I understood the minister to say that it was determined in the chemical laboratory.
In the seed laboratory. We have nothing to do with the chemical laboratory.
The minister does not seem to be in good temper.
I was explaining an answer to a question, and the very fact that the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) speaks of a 'chemical laboratory' shows that he misunderstood and I wish to set him right.

My hon. friend (Mr. Staples) asked the question how it was determined, and when the minister said it was in a laboratory, he asked how it was done. I said I understood that it was by actual count of the seed.
I did not understand the question to be put in that way.

I drew attention to the fact that the Act provided a standard, as I understood, of the number of noxious weed seeds permitted, this to be determined by actual count. As to the viability, of course, a certain percentage must germinate, and that must be tested in the laboratory. Thus, there must be two methods of reaching a standard of the seed that must be sold as No. 1. I thought the hon. member (Mr. Staples) was not getting the information he asked for.

If the hon. member wishes to answer the question instead of me, I suppose that is all right. The clause defines the character of the seed to be sold as No. 1. Whether the seed sold is of this character can only be determined in a seed laboratory, the large firms dealing in seeds have their own laboratories, and can determine whether the seeds they are selling are up to the mark or not. The consumer or small dealer who has bought from the wholesaler can, if he wishes, send samples to the seed laboratory of the department and these will be tested and a report furnished as rapidly as possible. Now, with regard to the point raised by the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith), in section 6 of the Act there is a list of what we call noxious weeds. We are adding one to the list by the present Bill. No seeds can he sold in Canada which contain seeds of any of these noxious weeds, unless the package is marked with the full name and address of the seller, and the common name of this kind or kinds of noxious weed seeds contained. Thus, if the farmer buys No. 1 seed, he knows it cannot contain any of these noxious weeds, or the merchant who

sells it is liable to prosecution and punishment. If the merchant chooses to sell seed which contains these noxious weed seeds, he must give his name and the name of the weed seed contained in the package. I do not think that any farmer with common sense would buy that kind of seed. We, therefore, have provided practically against the selling of seeds in Canada with any of these noxious weeds intermixed. From time to time we add to the list of prohibited noxious weed seeds, as we are doing to-day. These seeds are the particularly noxious ones. Of course, there are other injurious seeds, but not so bad as those in'-hr'erl in the list. Then, section 7 of the Bill defines what No. 1 seed is to be. We are not attempting-I hope we shall come to that by and by-to define No. 2 and No. 3 seed, or, perhaps ' rejected,' and let the farmers know what they are buying. However, we have not yet determined a safe definition of second or third class seed that we would like to put before the purchasing public. At present we think it safer -in fact the only safe way-for the farmer to buy No. 1 seed. I suppose the difference varies in different parts of the country. I am told that, the difference in price of a bushel of clover seed between No. 1 and other seed that does not come up to that standard, is not more than $1. We do not guarantee that these s-eeds shall not be found in seed that is sold as No. 1. But I can say that, roughly speaking, we make a test of something over 1,000 samples a year of the seeds which are marked No. 1, and not one half of one per cent has failed to come up to the standard. We get samples everywhere during the summer season, it is the duty of our inspectors to go about and buy samples and send them in to be tested, and especially do we aim at testing these No. 1 seeds, because they are the seeds that we want the farmers to buy. I think I am correct in saying that the No. 1 seed as marketed by the people of this country according to the laboratory test, is up to the standard.

I would like to inquire whether it is the intention of this Bill to increase the standard so as to provide for a less percentage of weeds than formerly existed. I have had some complaint from farmers in my riding that the standard is not sufficiently high to warrant them in getting pure seed. I recollect that when the Bill was brought in, there was a good deal of opposition to it, even by farmers, who complained that it was impossible to get a less percentage of weeds than the Bill provided for, and some considered it as a great hardship to the seed merchants to have 3o low a percentage, they said it was impossible, with the machinery available, for seedsmen to produce seed of the proper standard. I have had com-Mr. FISHER.
plaints from different sources that the standard is not sufficient to ensure the farmers getting good seed. Is it possible to get a less percentage of weed seed?

If my hon. friend will look at the Act, not the Bill, section 2 says:
The Governor in Council may make regulations to determine the maximum proportion of seeds of the weeds named in this Act that may be tolerated in any other seeds without affecting their character as being free from the seeds of the said weeds within the meaning of this Act.
That is the toleration clause. It is a little difficult to ensure absolute purity. In grains like oats and wheat we permit one in a pound. That means, roughly speaking, that there may be possibly one to the 1,500. The limit of toleration in grass 3eed and clover; is one in 1,500 by count. So if there is more than that, if there is one in 1,200 or 1,400, that seed would be regarded as impure, according to the Act. If there was only 1 in 1,600 or 1,700, that seed would be allowed to pass. I think the test is already pretty severe. Toleration is allowed chiefly for the purpose of permitting the accidental presence of these noxious weed seeds.
C-LARKE. Even that proportion would be dangerous in the dissemination of bad weeds.
We could require one in 2,000 instead of 1,500. Our object is to make the law just as strict as the trade can possibly bear.

I agree that the standard now is fairly high in regard to No. 1 seed. But there is No. 2 and No. 3. Does the minister think it would be impracticable to place a standard below which no seed should be sold? I think there should be some standard.

I would refer my hon. friend to section 8 of the Act:
No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale, for the purpose of seeding in Canada, any seeds cf timothy, alsike or red clover or any mixture containing the said seeds, if the seeds of the weeds named in this Act are present in greater proportion than 5 to 1,000 of the seed sold.
That is a statute, we cannot change it by regulation. The seeds named in this section are those I refer to in clauses 6 and 7, the noxious weeds. I do not think the trade could supply the farmers of Canada to-day if that clause was made more severe. We must improve the quality of seeds produced, so that the seedsmen may be able to buy seeds of that kind and quality.

I am pleased to learn that there is no practical standard below No. 1. But, would the minister not think it wise to go a little farther and prohibit any of those dangerous seeds, such as are named in No. 1 quality from being included in No. 2, and thus create a better standard?

We have no standard in No. 2 at all. We have fixed the standard at No. 1, and we have practically told the farmers that they ought to buy No. 1. As far as the Act is concerned there is no No. 2 or No. 3. No. 1 is called the government standard.
But you provide them with authority to sell another class of seed.

I am just informed that some of the seedsmen are selling a certain lower grade as government standard. If they are I will have to look after them and try and prevent it. I do not know just what the trick is or how I will prevent it, but I do not wish to have the standard below No. I ticketed with the name of the government. I shall have to look after these people, and if it is necessary I would like to amend the Act for the purpose of preventing them from doing that.

When this seed Bill was before the House two or three years ago, I drew the attention of the minister to the fact that the largest seed firms in Canada did not number their seeds at all. I have been in this business, not of late, but for many years, I have sold thousands of dollars worth of grass and clover seed; I have bought an equal amount from the big wholesale houses, but I have never bought a bushel of seed that was numbered. It was designated by a certain name. Grass and clover seed bore the names of certain animals, etc. These made it perfectly clear what the grade was, but it was never sold as No. 1. I do not know if there has been any change or not. If there has not been any change these men may continue to sell their seed under the names under which they sold it in the past and it would not be brought under the scope of the original Bill or the Bill before the House. I would like to know just how the minister deals with cases of that kind.

Since this Act came into force there has been much more temptation on the part of dealers to mark their seeds as No. 1. If my hon. friend will look at clause 7 of the Act he will see that that designation is not required, but that the clause includes No. 1 or any other designation which represents seed of first quality. For instance, if a man were to call seed ' prime ' or ' extra ' we would apply section 7 to it as well and haul him up if the seed
did not come up to the standard. Before this Act came into force and there was no standard at all for seeds, seedsmen offered their seeds under any name they chose, and there was nothing illegal about it. But since the Act has come into force, there is this standard, and we deal with the seed according to the names they apply. If they affix a name which may be included in that class, we deal with it accordingly.
Is there any clause in the Bill that compels a wholesale seedsman to designate his seed, 1, 2 or 3?
No.

He can call it ' wolf',
' fox', ' lynx', or any other name he likes, sell the seed under such name and not come under this section of the Act?
He will come under the Act if he sells seed under a name that would come under the designation of clause 7.
Suppose he calls it ' wolf ' or ' fox ' or ' lynx' ?
No, but successful farmers would not buy it under that name.
Well, they do buy it. I have bought and sold hundreds of thousands of bushels under names of that kind.

The farmers buy No. I as they are reasonably protected, and I think they get a fair quality of seed, or as good as they could reasonably expect. But, without a No. 2 or a No. 3 grade, if we so designate it by numbers, we could not supply the trade. A great many farmers are compelled to buy No. 2 or No. .3 because we cannot supply the trade with No. 1. I think it would not be going too far to ask the minister to have these very dangerous seeds extended to the other grades as well and prohibit the sale of them altogether. What are the names of the seeds which are prohibited in No. 1?

They are named in clause 6. They are prohibited in all seeds, and in clause 7 are those prohibited ones which are prohibited in No. 1. In regard to a second grade, when we were discussing the arrangement of this Bill, we examined into that, tout we did not wish to encourage the sale of any seeds except No. 1. We did not wish therefore to fix a standard which would toe pretty dangerous and very low. If we were making a standard of No. 2 slightly below No. 1, the relief that farmers and seedsmen must have would be very slight. If we made the difference very considerable, there would be a great temptation for many people to say: Well, No. 2 cannot be very bad, because there are a lot of numbers below No. 1, and I will buy it because it is cheaper. My hon. friend may

contend that the trade could not supply' the whole demand for No. 1. If that is largely true, it may be found to be a good sound argument in favour of creating a No. 2 grade, and I will look into that with the; greatest care. If I find, the facts such as will justify it and my officers can make a satisfactory description of a second grade,>
I would be rather disposed to introduce it into this Bill.

I think that the farmers should sow the best class of seed they can get, but the great difficulty we find is that when we buy No. 1 seed and it turns out to be of an inferior quality we cannot get back at the man who sells, it. Last spring a dealer in our town sold what was supposed to be first-class seed to a farmer, but which proved to be not nearly up to tire standard. The dealer was fined $2. He had bought it from a wholesale dealer in Toronto, but nothing further came of the matter and it was dropped. We find that this is the greatest trouble we have. Farmers are trying to use the very best seeds , they can get, but we are often deceived in the seed we buy, and it is not worth while to go after the seller .for all the fine that is imposed.
Did the farmer buy it for No. 1?
Yes, he bought it for No. 1 seed.	.
And the man was liable to a fine?
He was fined $2.
That brings up the question whether the fines are sufficiently severe. We publish the names of those who are fined, and that has a more deterrent effect than the actual amount of the penalty.
That would have more effect on the wholesalers than on the small retailers.
Yes. If the fines are not sufficient to deter, I have no hesitation in saying we will have to increase them.

I believe that the more dangerous seeds should be prohibited altogether. The sowdhistle is one of the most obnoxious weeds we have, and I regret to say that it is spreading through the province of Ontario.
Mr, SPROULE. It is a very common thing to sell two or three grades of seed, and while the good farmer will take nothing but the best grade, others are not so careful. Now, clause 6 provides that the package must have the full name and address of the seller with the name and kind of seeds and the common names of the weed contained in the seeds. I do not Mr. FISHER.
think that law is complied with, because if it were nobody would buy the weeds if he knew they were in the seed.
The very fact that the name of these weeds is on the package is an open warning to the farmers not to buy, and they don't buy.
But I do not think it is put on the package.

Then it is sold in contravention of the law. If a man has a quantity of seeds which contain these weeds, he can sell them legally by putting the names of the weeds on the package, but if he does, of course nobody will buy them.1
It is a common practice to offer for sale different grades of seed, and people buy them.
I repeat that the sale of wild mustard and sow-thistle seed by the dealer or the farmer or any one else should be absolutely prohibited.
Wild mustard is prohibited in clause 6 of the Bill.
That is a good thing.
How is it that every year you get wild mustard in your sugar beet and turnip seed?
Because, unfortunately, the Act is violated.
If a farmer goes to a store and wants half a bushel of seed, and it is taken out of a bin and put in a bag, there is nothing to indicate that it contains weeds.
The seller would have to put the name of the weed on the package in which he sells, as on the bin.

Now that the different sections of the Bill have been carried, I want to have a little talk with the Minister .of Agriculture about the destruction of noxious weeds throughout this Dominion. This Bill prohibits the sale of seeds that contain noxious seeds, which is in the right direction; but, unfortunately, with all the care that- may be taken under this Bill, they will still be sold. The country, generally speaking, is becoming very much polluted with noxious weeds, and there is no question which is giving the farmers of this country more anxiety at the present time. The government of Manitoba has been exercising the greatest care on this subject; it has placed on the statute-book the most drastic law it could think out; but I believe that the Dominion government, which has a greater revenue at its command, a revenue gathered especially from the agriculturists of this country, could well afford to spend some of that

money in enforcing a law that would start at the very root of this unfortunate condition of affairs. It takes an enormous amount of money to enforce a law of this kind. Those who have their farms polluted with these noxious weeds suffer great loss, perhaps through their own fault, or through not knowing at first how injurious certain seeds would be. For instance, in the section of the country which I have the honour to represent, and in which the sow thistle prevails, the farmers did not realize for a number of years that it was as injurious as it has turned out to be. If the Minister of Agriculture is alive to the interests of the farmers, he should follow up this legislation with a law for the eradication of noxious weeds throughout this country. To my mind, this is one of the biggest questions the farmers of the west have to deal with. I do not know whether the minister has sucn intentions or not. If he has not, I would like to do my utmost to start him thinking along that line. The government of Manitoba has expended enormous sums of money in the attempt to destroy noxious weeds in that province; but a little province like that, without a stick of timber or a foot of land to derive a revenue from, cannot do much compared with this government, and I think it should use some of the money which it collects from the farmers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta as well as those of the other provinces, and give it back to them in the way of administering a law that would eradicate these weeds from the farms of the country.
Mr FISHER The subject which my hon. friend has brought up is one of the vastest importance and has a very wide hearing. The destruction of weeds on the land has been dealt with by the various provincial legislatures, including that of his own province of Manitoba.
I know that; I have the law before me; but it takes an enormous amount of money to enforce that law.
But it is not enforced, unfortunately.
I will venture to say that there is not another government in this Dominion making the efforts the government of Manitoba is to enforce the law.
I am glad to hear it, but that is only a reflection on the other governments. This is a matter almost entirely of municipal control. I doubt very much if we could enforce a law in regard to it.

That is the unfortunate part of it. When a municipality appoints an officer to deal with the law, and that
officer goes on to his neighbour's farm and orders him to cut down a field of grain and destroy it, that is where the trouble begins. If we had a general law, enforced by the officers of this government, it would have a better effect, and would not probably cause ill feeling among neighbours.

It does not require a Dominion law for that. The government of Manitoba could amend that feature of its law and provide efficient inspectors as well as the Dominion government could. As a matter of fact, that question has been dealt with by municipal regulation, which is a purely provincial matter, and which the Dominion government cannot interefere with. I am very dubious whether we could frame an Act which would enable us to enter upon a man's land and deal with noxious weeds on that land; and we certainly could not frame an Act which would cover the public highways, as the provincial and municipal authorities could. Any Act we framed would be very much restricted, even if it were not declared ultra vires of this parliament. I am not going to give a legal opinion on that point, but I can well understand the practical difficulties the Dominion government would have in enforcing such a law; and when we find that most of the provinces of the Dominion have such laws, which, according to my hon. friend, are not enforced, and which apparently are not enforced because they are not right
It takes too much money to enforce them. Why should not this government lend some aid in that respect?

I am perfectly willing to lend any aid within my power; but in this case, as in many others, where the provincial authorities are derelict in their duty, people appeal to us to 'do what the provincial authorities should do. The proper course is to keep their own provincial authorities up to the mark. My hon. friend had better deal with the authorities of the province he comes from.
I would like to ask what means are taken under this law to ascertain what seeds will germinate?
We have a germinating test. The seeds are put into a germinating plant or machine which shows at once or very shortly what seeds will germinate.
How are the dealers or farmers to know what seeds will germinate?
They can make the test themselves if they choose, or they can send samples here and have them tested.

I appreciate very much what [DOT]the department has been doing in the last

three years. We must admit that the farmers are improving greatly and still we can acknowledge that weeds are increasing. That is natural and I am afraid it will continue. We have new seeds and probably worse seeds coming all the time and I think the government should try to help the farmers to eradicate the weeds and keep them out. My hon. friend here seems to think the law should be very stringent. I claim it should not and I ask my hon. friend from Manitoba how it worked in the west when the law said that you could go out and mow down a farmer's field of grain if it contained many weeds. That is beneficial to the farmer with the clean farm, but we must also look after the poor man. They had to amend the law which allowed the elevator men to retain the screenings.
Where was the law amended?

The principal of the agricultural college in Manitoba was sent out by the premier to ascertain if the farmers were content to take chances and get the screenings. He found that the great majority of the farmers were and they got the screenings back, I think it was an injustice to the farmers to have to leave their screenings at the elevators or mills for no doubt the elevator men kept a great amount of the screenings. While we are helping ourselves in some ways we may be injuring the country in others. I believe the government are doing all they can at the present time and I think they should try and increase the help they give to the farmers as the country increases. Let us give credit where credit is due. Ten or twenty or thirty years ago, we had not the seed tests we have to-day and I admit we did not need such tests, but, we have as much need now for the improved tests as for any other aid to agriculture. I, as a farmer, would ask the government to try to do everything possible to eradicate the weeds and keep the farms clear of them. They should encourage the farmers to sow nothing but No. 1, or the best seed. The farmers in too many cases do not properly clean the seeds which they raise, many seeds are resowed from improper cleaning. If the farmers are educated to sow the best and none but the best we will improve very much.

I assure my hon. friend I appreciate his views. We are watching very closely any opportunity to increase the stringency of these laws without unduly or unnecessarily interfering with the private business of the people. Before this Act was passed, there was nothing to prevent the refuse seeds of other countries being dumped on Canada and sold here. Since this Act has been in force the pro-Mr. BEST.
visions of the Act apply to seeds imported into _ Canada and any one selling seeds not coming up to the requirements of this Act, is mulcted and punished. The result is that the quality of the seeds imported into Canada from other countries has vastly improved, and we are, I think, safe in that way from the introduction of seeds from abroad which sometimes were brought into the country. It is well known that some of the worst and most noxious weeds we have in Canada were imported from abroad in seeds. That kind of thing can hardly occur under the operations of this Act and we are watching all the time where we can improve our legislation and its administration so as to take advantage of every opportunity of increasing the safeguards.
Is it not a fact that in many cases retail merchants would keep a good tested sample in the store, but would sell another grade to the farmer?
The inspectors inspect the seeds being sold, and any farmer can at once send a sample of the seed he has bought to the department and get it tested, without cost.
As a rule the farmers do not take much pains in getting the seed tested. I do not see anything in the Act that will protect the farmers or prevent the merchants from selling that inferior seed.
If the merchant sells seed that does not come up to the quality established by the Act he is liable to a penalty.

For some time I have been watching the seed sold in our section and I do not think there is any improvement. I do not know where the leak is, but the Act does not seem to have the effect people anticipated.
Mr. FISHER, Our inspectors have taken samples of all kinds of seeds in every part of the country, and the result of testing those samples has been to show very marked improvements in the quality of the seeds offered; but of course if farmers will not take the trouble to give us an opportunity to protect them, we cannot protect them against their will.

I think there is a very important omission in the Act. Farmers are not botanists. Very often, even with the aid of books sent out from the department, they can scarcely recognize and name the weeds which they see growing. I would like to know how many retail merchants or farmers are able to take a handful of grain and name the seeds mixed with it. I suggested on a former occasion that any person who retailed seed under this Act should be compelled to have .in his place of business, one of those

cards of small bottles containing the different weed seeds, so that when a farmer buys seed he can compare it with the sample and know what he is really buying. This question of weeds in the west is very important. I think the yield has been reduced nearly one quarter in some cases, owing to noxious weeds. That matter should be looked into very carefully and every attempt made to check the increase of weeds.

The samples of seeds of the different weeds are available not only for seed merchants, but for anybody else. I understand that. But I do not know that we could very well say that everybody who sells seeds should be compelled to have such a cabinet. We supply them at a mere nominal figure. But a man may sell seeds this year and not next year. The farmer has a protection that is far betterhe need not trust to his eyesight or his knowledge of seeds; he can send a sample to the seed laboratory here, and it will be tested and a report sent to him immediately, so that he will know absolutely, by the official record, the character of the seed he is buying.

It may be that a farmer has to go twenty miles to town to buy seed, and buys it, perhaps, to sow next day. How can he wait to send a sample to the department? subtopic: MANITOBA FISHERIES COMMISSION.
MANITOBA FISHERIES COMMISSION.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire for a few moments to call the attention of the House to a report w'hich was laid on the table a few days ago of the fishery commission which was appointed to investigate the fisheries in Manitoba. I regret very much that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) is not in his place. I regret to have to discuss this matter in his absence, b!ut the question is of such importance that I feel justified in asking the House to bear with me for a few moments while I review this report. During the holidays there was an interview published in one of the Monti eal papers, given, I presume, by one of the officials. If it had not been for that, interview, I do not think I wrtuld havd asked the House to have listened to any remarks of mine just at the present time, but, in justice to myself, however, I feel that I must ask the House to listen to what I have to say in regard to this report. An interview was published in the Montreal ' Star ' of December 22, 1909, as follows:

subtopic: MANITOBA FISHERIES COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Ottawa, December 22.-The commission appointed some months ago to inquire into the question of Manitoba fisheries and to investigate allegations as to undue advantages being possessed by the Fish Trust, has completed an interim report. The appointment to the bench of one of the commissioners, Mr. Metcalfe, somewhat disorganized the inquiry, which is by no means completed, but it will be resumed next summer.
It is learned that the evidence so far taken, and which is embodied in the interim report is not of a character justifying some of the allegations made. The commission, however, is not in a position to make any recommendations till the inquiry is completed.
I desire to call the attention of the House to the fact that every allegation, every charge that was made on the floor of this House last year by myself has been borne out by the report brought in by the commission, which I hold in my hand. More than that, the commission not only has corroborated everything I said here, but it has brought in recommendations far more drastic than anything I suggested. This is a question that has agitated the people of Manitoba during the last twelve or fourteen years. I was perhaps more conversant with this matter than many others, and I have repeatedly petitioned and had personal interviews with the Fishery Department, both with its minister and officials, but up to the time that this commission was appointed I have failed to secure any redress of or any consideration for the grievances and complaints of the fishermen and residents of Manitoba. I want to say in justice to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries that this is a matter in which he has taken considerable interest. I believe, Sir, that he has done what was possible to secure a fair and honest report, and I want to do justice to that hon. gentleman in this regard. The report was laid on the table by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) a few days ago, and I intend placing it on ' Hansard ' that the people of the west may know exactly what has' taken place. This report is not in printed form and cannot be circulated in any other way.
Interim Report.
To the honourable
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa.
Sir,-We, the commissioners appointed by order in council to investigate the waters of Manitoba and the west, have completed our first investigation of the waters of the province of Manitoba and have the honour to present an interim report, consisting of two parts:
1st. Certain important conclusions, based on the evidence received at the series of sittings held during the past summer.
2nd. Recommendations, with a view to such changes in the regulations governing the Manitoba Fisheries as appear necessary from the facts brought before the commission in the evidence.

Conclusions of the Commission.
1.	We have reached the conclusion that all the lakes of Manitoba have been over-fished, and that some of the more valuable species such as the whitefish and the yellow pickerel hare decreased very seriously in size and in abundance, and that the sturgeon-the most valuable fish found in these water-is 'on the point of extinction and can only be preserved by stringent measures.
I want to -call the attention of the House to the fact that -during my remarks last session I pointed out the very facts that have been so strongly supported in this report. The Minister of Marine, through the promptings of one of the -officials who sat at his side, -denied that there was any fear of the depletion of the waters of Lake Winnipeg. I took the opportunity of asking the minister at that time to hold a searching investigation into these matters. The investigation was held and has justified what I said on that occasion. The report goes on to say:
2.	The evidence shows that tiie fishery laws have not been generally observed, both in regard to quantity of net used, size of mesh, &c., although the close seasons have in our opinion been observed by the majority.
3.	We have abundant evidence that the Manitoba fisheries have been unduly controlled by foreign fish operators, who have dictated the prices of fish and have secured the major portion of the profits.
That is also a matter that I have pressed upon the Fishery Department during the last ten or twelve years. I have proven beyond a doubt that the fisheries in Manitoba were controlled absolutely by th-e American Fish Trust, or the Booth Fish Packing Company of Chicago, But in face of the evidence that I have submitted from time to time to the Fishery Department I have failed to receive any redress for the fishermen through any regulations which would have prevented these men from ruining our great fisheries. The consequence is that to-day we find this great fishery, once the greatest whitefish fishery on this continent, in a depleted condition, depleted to the detriment of our own settlers, while American citizens have made fortunes out of these fisheries. The investigation which has been made corroborates everything that I have stated year after year and which I stated to this House last year. The report goes on to say:
The people of Manitoba have benefited little from these great lake fisheries. Moreover inferior grades of fish have been sold in the Canadian market, while the better graces, including the larger size of fish, have been exported to the United States markets.
That is another point that I have emphasized time after time. The best fish that were taken out of Lake Winnipeg and 85i
our other lakes were exported to the American markets and the Canadians had to be satisfied with the culls. We had to pay a very much increased price even for the cull fish on account of the quantity that was exported to the American market out of our own country. It goes on to say:
It cannot he denied that the main market has been hitherto in the United States and the home market has been limited. With the wonderful development of Canada and the rapid growth of new towns in the west, the demand for fish is rapidly increasing, it is imperative that every effort should be made to restore these fisheries to their former plenitude, in order to provide a great staple food for the future population of the Dominion.
What a reflection this report is upon the foresight and wisdom of the Marine and Fisheries Department. The idea that this once great fishery has been allowed to bq depleted, and now the commissioners come and recommend that this country must spend tens of thousands of dollars in an effort to replenish this lake after allowing the Americans to take the fish from it and send them to the American market. The report goes on:
VVe are convinced that a minimum size limit for the more important food fishes is absolutely necessary. We therefore recommend that certain sizes of fish should he specified in tue regulations, below which nofish can be legally captured. We also recommend that the legal mesh of various nets should he increased.
It is essential, in our opinion, that fish, whether caught in Manitoba waters or elsewhere, should not be possessed, bought, sold or handled during the close season, provided by the regulations; but dealers having legally-caught fish in storage might, in our view, be allowed to hold them in storage under authority of a written permit issued by the inspector of fisheries.
We have found that the existing regulations regarding the possession and the sale of fish in close season have been openly and universally violated.	,
This, Mr. Speaker, is another matter that has been called to the attention of the Fisheries Department year after year by myself and others, and we have always failed to gain support or sympathy from that department. It has seemed impossible to get the Fisheries Department to take hold of this question in a business way and to protect the fisheries in the interest of the Canadian consumer and the Canadian fisherman, while on the other hand everything possible seems to have been done in the interest of the great American trust, who,~ one would imagine, had control of the Fishery Department here at Ottawa.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL WATERWAYS CANAL AND CONSTRUCTION COMPANY.
speechtext: I feel it my duty to call the attention of the House to the fact that I have received a communication from the city of Edmonton urging that this Bill should not be allowed to pass in any form, which I think would mean its present form, which would give to the company any exclusive right or any right of control over the river Saskatchwan. The Bill is very broad in its terms. It gives power not only to build a canal from Lake Superior, or from the Pigeon river to Rainy river, but it seeks to give control of the waters of the Rainy lake and the^ Rainy river and then to make a connection between the Lake of the Woods and the Winnipeg river, so connecting with Lake Winnipeg. Then it seems to give control, and I think it does by its terms give control over the waters of Cedar lake and Cross lake, which are parts of the Saskatchewan river, and also over the Saskatchewan river, the Assiniboine river and I think possibly Lake Manitoba and Lake Winnipeg with power to exact tolls on goods transported over these waterways. I think my hon. friend will, on consideration, see that while it might be quite proper and perhaps desirable in the public interest that a company should be given power to build canals which should connect these waterways, it would not be proper to give to a private company any control of any kind or description over these great navigable waters in the western part of the province of Ontario and in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. I therefore feel it my duty to oppose the second reading of the Bill.

speechtext:
' It seems to me that, in view of the change of policy of the provinces and the Dominion in regard to water-powers and water highways to keep them as much as possible under the control of the government, and not give them over to the control of private individuals, we should be doing something not in the best interests of the Dominion, or of the provinces, if we granted the powers proposed in this Bill. I agree with the Minister of Public Works that such a Bill should not pass this House. The hon. member (Mr. Conmee) says that any safeguards necessary can be added. But the object of the incorporators is to get the right to build and then they will take chances of afterwards being able to secure the privileges under the plea that the charter gives the right to build these dams and therefore they are entitled to avail themselves of the powers of their charter. A corporation is given certain corporate rights, and I think it is generally held that they must be allowed to avail themselves of the powers given in their charter and go on with the undertaking. Thus it may have the effect of forcing the hand of a province or of a municipality where otherwise they would refrain from giving the power asked for by the company. Hence, I think this Bill is wrong, radically wrong. Then, as I understand it, this is an international affair. Why should a private

corporation control an international stream or any portion of it? The two countries might do it by agreement, but to give the power to a private corporation, I think, is radically wrong. This is a portion of the country that we know very little about; we do not know what is to be taken possession of up there. We have a commission appointed to look after these things-water-powers, streams, timber and other natural resources, and we should refrain from tying their hands more than has already been done until they have developed a policy that will be suitable and that will be assented to by the provincial and federal governments.
