When the House Tose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was referring to the report brought down by the Fisheries Commission, signed by Prof. Prince, Mr. D. F. Reed and Mr. Hugg. I do not intend to read this report to the House to-night, because I dealt Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
with the matter to some extent last session. However, I wish again to emphasize the recommendations and the findings of this report so that the House may be seized to some extent of the situation so far as our Manitoba fisheries are concerned. At one time Lake Winnipeg was probably the greatest whitefish lake on this continent, and when you realize that to-day it is almost depleted you will understand what has taken place during the last fifteen years, notwithstanding the innumerable protests, private and public, made to the government against the operation of the American fish trust in these waters. For the information of the House, I may say that the Booth Fish Packing Company of Chicago, the great octopus that has fastened its tentacles on every lake and on every sheet of fish-producing water in Canada, has done more to destroy these great fisheries of Manitoba than all other influences combined. And, Mr. Speaker, the Booth Company has been able to accomplish this through the agency and influence of some of our Canadian citizens. The law was such that Americans could not obtain licenses in these waters, but they used Canadians for their purpose and they formed what was then called the Dominion Fish Company, which was presided over by Capt. Wm. Robinson, of Selkirk, and in this way licenses were obtained to fish these waters in defiance of the laws of Canada. That the department was made aware time after time that the Dominion Fish Company was really the Booth Fish Packing Company of Chicago can be demonstrated from the files of the department. But the representations made to the minister time after time by representative men, and in petitions from the settlers along the lake who were being deprived of their fishing rights, were all of no avail. It seemed impossible to obtain from the department any redress for the people. After a long and tedious fight for years, the Fishery Department at last realized that there was something wrong, and instituted an inquiry; and we have here to-night the result of that inquiry before us.
One of the reasons why I am troubling the House at the present time is that this is not the first report of a royal commission that has been filed in the Fisheries Department. In 1884 or 1885, at the request of the settlers of Lake Winnipeg, assisted by myself, the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Sir Charles Hibbert Dupper, granted a commission. We_eomplained at that time that the Americans were controlling our waters, violating the law by setting out double the quantity of nets allowed, polluting the waters with dead fish and depleting the waters. That commission reported, but there were influences at work sufficiently strong to stay the hand

of the department, and the report has never been acted upon, although it proved every contention made at the time in three or four hundred sheets of foolscap. Up to the present time that report remains a dead letter, I presume locked up in the archives of the Fishery Department. It is for fear that a similar result may happen to the report of this commission that I have brought this matter before the House tonight, that the House may realize that the American fish trust has friends at court sufficiently strong, even in the face of a report as drastic as this one is, perhaps to influence the government against carrying into effect the recommendations of their commissioners. I tnust, however, that no influences will be allowed to interfere with the minister or the government in seeing that the spirit of this report is carried into effect. I cannot say that I agree with one or two of the recommendations, which I consider to be rather drastic at the present time. The report recommends that Lake Winnipeg be closed from 1911, and yet Captain Robertson, of Winnipeg, who was president of the Dominion Fish Company, which was part of the Booth Fish Packing Company of Chicago, is to-day getting ready a fleet of 26 sailboats and two tugs to fish in that lake next summer. If some measure is not taken to make that impossible, it will mean almost the total destruction of the fisheries of Lake Winnipeg next summer. The companies realize that public opinion has been aroused on this question and is demanding that the government take action to protect this great fishery. They realize that next summer will be the last opportunity they will have, perhaps for some years to come, and if some power does not intervene, the damage that will be done will be almost irreparable. I trust therefore that the government will take steps to see that such restrictions are put on the fishing operations on Lake Winnipeg for next summer as will make it impossible for any combination virtually to destroy that great fishery. The system of fishery inspection, supervision and licensing carried out by the department requires, we are convinced, to be radically changed if effective enforcement of the law is to be secured. The local officers we have found to be inefficient, poorly paid, without proper means of transportation and not properly instructed in their duties. They habitually fail to report breaches of the law in their own localities. Even when such officers do report to the district inspector, it frequently occurs that no instructions relating to the case are given, owing to law methods in the carrying on of the inspector's work. Serious delays occur in this connection and very frequently the evidence that the law has been broken is not available when the instructions come to hand. We found that the chief inspector at a critical season of the year was engaged upon hatchery business, and was thus compelled to neglect the proper duties of his office. If it is absolutely necessary that the officer named should be absent frequently from his office, a deputy should be in charge.
The patrol of Lake Winnipeg by the inspector cannot be effective as at present carj ried out, his boat the 1 Lady of the Lake, being most unsuitable for such work.
During the discussion last year I drew the attention of the Hotuse to the fact that this government had purchased for the fishery inspector for patrol purposes a large steamer called the ' Lady of the Lake,' which cost the country some $8,000, and, according to returns brought down, about $7,000 a year to run it. It is the height of absurdity to have a boat of this kind on Lake Winnipeg. It is utterly useless for the purpose it was bought for, as I then pointed out, and as the commission now affirms:
Its large size gives early warning of its approach to all persons engaged in illegal operations. A small swift tug or launch should be provided on Lake Winnipeg, and indeed on each of the more important lakes of the province.
10. We found it very difficult to get reliable statistics as to the catches of fish on the various lakes, and recommend that sworn returns should be required as to the quantities of all fish taken out of the water

I might draw the attention of the House to the fact that this was one of my contentions last year, that as the reports were made up it was impossible for any one to arrive at a fair idea of the quantities of the different kind of fish taken out of these' waters.
-such returns to be furnished by each licensee to the inspector twice a year, on the 31st March and 30th of September, and that failure to furnish the said returns shall deprive the licensee so failing of the right to a new license until his default shall be remedied. We further recommend that the inspectors be required to analyse and summarize the said

returns, so as to indicate clearly the quantities of each kind of fish taken from each of the principal bodies of water in the * province.
I shall not read any more of the report. I wished to plaee that part of the report on record so that the country may understand some of the features I have been discussing here. But I wish to emphasize as clearly as I can, the fact that the danger is that the department is apparently not strong enough to carry out even the recommendations of this commission. I find that in the days gone by when we have endeavoured to get grievances such as these rectified there have been influences at work which have made it almost impossible to do anything and I trust the government will take this matter up earnestly and see that the spirit of this report is carried out.
I wish to refer to the report on Lac du Bonnet. I drew attention to the fact that this is an important sturgeon breeding ground and urged the necessity of closing it against all commercial fishing. This report, like the other, verified everything I said then and contains a recommendation along the same line. It has been recommended that the export of sturgeon from Manitoba waters should1 be prohibited and this is a phase of the question which I wish to emphasize. If we are to protect the sturgeon of Lake Manitoba, Lake Winnipeg and Lac du Bonnet, the only way to protect it is to prohibit the export. According to this report and my recommendation the settlers around the lake should be allowed to fish for sturgeon. It is a great food fish. We have along this lake 600 or 700 settlers. In the lower part of the lake we have a French settlement at St. George and they draw their food supplies largely from this lake. If the lake is allowed to be . fished for commercial purposes, one year would, I think, thoroughly deplete this lake of sturgeon. This report has verified that fact, and I wish to emphasize, as I stated before, the necessity of the government prohibiting the export of sturgeon from Manitoba. I desire to call the attention of the government to the absolute necessity of taking action this summer in protecting Lake Winnipeg and Lac du Bonnet. If this report is allowed to stand over until the fishing season starts, until the great companies have secured their licenses, there will be a repetition of what has been done in former years by the large commercial companies. Last year I think some 2,500,000 pounds of whitefish were taken out of Lake Winnipeg, I believe that if the quantity this year is limited to that amount no great harm could occur to the lake this summer, until the commission completes its work. This is an interim report, I understand the commission is ordered back to Lake Winnipeg to complete its task. If that limitation is not im-

posed, then, with the introduction of this great plant I spoke of, together with the plants now on the lake, this amount can be trebled and 8,000,000 or 9,000,000 pounds can be taken out. That would be a serious matter for the lake and the settlers, and I trust that action will be taken along these lines to make it impossible for these great companies to destroy our great lake fisheries.
One of the modes of operation of the American companies has been to take advantage of the American customs regulations. All fish caught in American nets have been permitted to go into the United States free of duty, while fish taken in nets owned by Canadians have been met with a duty of a quarter of a cent a pound At the boundary line. You can realize what that means, it gives the absolute control of the American market into the hands of the Booth Fish Packing Company of Chicago. The manner in which they did this was well known to the Fisheries Department, because it has been brought to their attention time after time. The Booth Company organized a Canadian branch and called it the Dominion Fish Company. They put Captain Robinson, a Canadian, at its head. This company obtained a license from the Dominion government to fish, and signed a declaration when they got their license that they were the actual owners of the plant and gear fishing in these waters according to our law. Then, when the fish reached the American markets, the Americans took the oath that these fish were caught in American nets. The consequence was that our law was violated and the American law was violated, but the Americans got their fish in free, while the Canadians were met by a duty of one-quarter of a cent per pound. That is one of the modes of operation of the American combination, and it is one upon which the government should take some action. I trust that the Fisheries Department will see to it that the spirit of this report is put into operation at the earliest possible opportunity, and that the interests of our settlers will be protected and winter fishing under wise and fair regulations provided for.

It seems to me that the evil antedates the action of the fishermen. The evil starts first in the Fishery Department in giving licenses to a number of individuals away in advance of settlement to control certain important and valuable fishing grounds and fishing waters for a mere trifle. We have had it brought to the attention of this House more than once. Take the case of Mr. McNee and others associated with him, and Mr. Markey, of Montreal. They have got license after license from the govern-

ment extending over a number of years and covering operations on Lake Winnipeg, Great Slave lake, Great Bear lake and Lesser Slave lake, Hudson bay and various other small lakes and rivers throughout that country for a mere trifle, and turned around and sold their leases to others who are trying to get control of them to the disadvantage of the .settler when he came there and of the country as well. These parties are usually associated with Americans. And, after catching the fish in Canada, they evade the customs at the boundaries and take the fish into fthe United States free. A Canadian, wishing to export fish, must pay the duty, and so he is unable to compete. Two years ago- and I believe the same thing goes on today-the Buffalo Fish Company was carrying on operations of this kind on Georgian bay. The law of the United States, I understand, provides that fish caught by Americans are admitted to the United States free of duty. So they come here and get a license, and are able to take the oath that the fish have been caught by Americans, and so they get the advantage of the American market, while the Canadian is shut out. As might be expected, the result is that these operations are all carried on by Americans who hire Canadians to do the work for them. If you go into the Marine and Fisheries Department you will find that license after license has been issued, some as low as $8 a year, and from that up to $100 a year, through which these people control these valuable fisheries to the detriment of our own people. And the licenses are renewable.
Now, is that right or is it wrong? If the government wishes to manage the department in a wise and business-like way, would they carry out this policy? No. Who are the people who get the benefit of this system? The speculators and the operators. And so we have these licenses covering these privileges in the Peace River district, in Slave lake, in the Hudson bay, in the Nelson river and in all that northern country-all held by men who never worked as fishermen, but who are the managers of the concerns and who manage them so as to make large sums of money out of them. And all the money that is made outside of that of the exploiter, goes into the hands of the Americans. Do not the government agree with me that the principle is wrong and that, until settlement or other interests make it necessary, these fisheries should be reserved? I think it is time the government looked into these questions. I cannot imagine for a moment that they do not understand the facts. They cannot be ignorant of the way this system is carried on and of the evils that must result. But, because some of their political friends, who are always-I was
going to say on the graft, but perhaps I should rather say with speculative aim in view, improper speculative aim in view- they are allowed to carry on these nefarious operations. It is time that this should be stopped, and, unless the government put a stop to it soon; they will be obliged to do generally what they are doing now in many cases, providing breeding establishments, at a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars to stock the depleted waters of our country-depleted not by our own citizens, but by those living outside the country altogether. This matter has been brought to my attention over and over again by the fishermen of the Georgian bay. But it has seemed io be impossible to control the government. Sometimes, it is said, that the banks own the government If we consider the Marine and Fisheries Department, I should be inclined to say that this class of fishermen seem to control it, and citizens of this country have no power to bring about right management.
May I ask a question? To which government does he refer when speaking of fishing in the lakes of Ontario?
The federal government.
Is not the hon. member aware of the fact that no person is allowed to fish in the waters of Ontario without the license of the provincial government also?

The Ontario government impose a license for purposes of revenue, but it is the Dominion government that regulates the size of the mesh of nets and other matters in relation to fisheries. Besides, this government has control of Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan and all the country to the north, with their great and valuable lakes. And they are giving these practically interminable licenses just as in the past. From what I know, I am inclined to believe that the provincial government is desirous of conserving these valuable rights for the people of the province, but they are unable to do so because of the conflict of jurisdiction between the federal and provincial governments upon this question of fishery rights. Several times I have called the attention of the government in this matter, and have asked if they could not hurry up their arrangements so as to reach some definite conclusion, that it might be known to which authority these rights actually belong. The federal authority has control and is exercising these rights-not in Ontario, for, since the decision of the Privy Council on the subject, the government of Ontario has exercised control. But it is being carried on in other parts of the Dominion by the department here and those who have these rights from the department, enjoy the benefit of the fisheries.

I cannot pretend to have the knowledge of the Fisheries Department to enable me to supply the information sought by my hon. friend from Manitoba (Mr. Bradbury). But his remarks will be brought to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. As to what my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has to say, he mentioned one or two of what he called glaring instances in which the rights of the people had been sacrificed and the privileges given. He spoke of a lease given to Mr. McNee, and another given to Mr. Markey. I suppose the hon. gentleman is aware that these leases were cancelled long ago, and the privileges taken away, because onerous conditions which had been attached to the leases, were not fulfilled by the holders. My hon. friend will find, I think, that in the Marine and Fisheries Department, in this respect as in others, a great change and reorganization has taken place, and most of what he has been talking about has not been done for several years past.
Mr, SPROULE. If the minister will excuse me, I was on the Public Accounts Committee the year before last, when we discussed the matter, and it was admitted by the party who was brought before the committee, that he had the license.

I admit that such licenses were issued at one time, but few licenses are now being issued in the way he has described. Old licenses issued years ago were perhaps described fairly by the hon. member. But the two he mentioned in particular were cancelled, because, as I have said, onerous conditions were not fulfilled-the conditions were so onerous that the parties were not able to fulfil them. That showed that the government which issued those licenses was safeguarding the public interests sufficiently to require the licensees to do certain things which they were not able to do, and consequently the licenses were cancelled. This has been the case with other licenses. The present Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in the reorganization of his department, which he has carried on in such a splendid manner, and which he is continuing to improve, so far as his health permits, has also dealt with the issuing of these fishery licenses.

It did not appear quite clear to me what my hon. friend is asking for. He seems to point out a grievance, but the main grievance he pointed out, if I understand him, was something over which this parliament and government have no control. He informs us that fishermen fishing in Lake Winnipeg and in some of those inland waters, are allowed to send their fish into the United States Mr. SPROULE.
market without paying any duty, providing the fish are caught in American nets and American bottoms. Now this is not a matter which this government can control, although it may seem a hardship to Cana dian fishermen.

The law of this country is very distinct, that no man is permitted to fish in Canada except he is a. British subject, and except he is the actual owner of his boats and gear. Now, if he is the actual owner, how can an American own the nets.? As soon as the department becomes aware that these fish are going into that country free of duty, on account of the American owning the nets, then! it is the duty of the department to cancel the licenses.

It may be their duty. The business, as pointed out by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), appears to be fraudulent, because these fishermen are representing themselves to be Canadian fishermen catching fish in Canadian waters, and then in the United States, he says, they produce evidence that the fish are caught ini American nets. If that is the case, of course there is fraudulent fishing carried on, and that would be good reason for cancelling the licenses. I have no doubt that if a case of that kind is brought to the attention of the minister, the license will be immediately cancelled.
I have brought cases before them from time to time.

No one proposes to stop granting licenses altogether. I assume from the fact that the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) supports the Ontario government that grants the licenses, he is not opposed to granting licenses.

I take the ground that there is no justification, from settlement or any other cause, to grant licenses to fish, whether it be to fish on the Great Slave lake or in Lesser Slave lake, or in Hudson bay.
I understand my hon. friend was also criticising the method of granting licenses in the Georgian bay as well as in the great lakes to the north.

I said fishing had been carried on there to the detriment of the people, and I spoke of the evils that have resulted. I also snoke of the far distant country where there was no settlement, and where it would be a wrong thing to do.

If my hon. friend will examine the law and the regulations in the department, he will find that the licenses

granted in this northern country must be operated or they are subject to cancellation at any time. It is a condition on which licenses are granted, and if there are cases in which the licenses are not being operated, then they are subject to cancellation. It is easy to work up complaints in a matter of this kind, but hon. members ought to be in a position to propose a remedy. If they are serious about this matter, if they have any complaint for which they can find a remedy, then I would like to hear what the remedy is. I listened carefully to the hon. member for Selkirk, but it did not appear to me clear that he had anything to propose to the department that would remedy these complaints.

I want to inform the hon. gentleman that I was simply emphasizing the report of the commission appointed by the government to investigate this matter. I approve of the commission. The commission brought in very drastic recommendations, and I was asking that the government should carry out those recommendations in the spirit of the report. I also pointed out that there was another commission appointed under the old government in 1884-5, and the report of that commission is lying in the department to-day; it was never carried out, it was burked by the influence of this American fish trust.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Harbours and rivers, Prince Edward Island -Belfast pier-renewals and repairs on pier head and general repairs to approach-revote of $1,800 lapsed, $2,000.

The commission brought in very drastic recommendations, and I was asking that the government should carry out those recommendations in the spirit of the report. I also pointed out that there was another commission appointed under the old government in 1884-5, and the report of that commission is lying in the department to-day; it was never carried out, it was burked by the influence of this American fish trust.']

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
This is to reconstruct portions *of the face of the pier at Halliday's wharf, and to make some other general repairs. The total estimated cost of these repairs is $3,000. Some work was done and there was an appropriation last year of $3,000, of which amount there has been spent $1,200.
Belle River harbour - repairs to and strengthening works oil either side of entrance, $3,000.
This is asked for by the resident engineer to strengthen the works on either side of the harbour entrance.
Where is this?

It is in Queens county, Prince Edward Island.
Brudenell-wharf on north side of river- revote of $2,000 lapsed, $5,400.

This is to make provision for the construction of a wharf at
Brudenell. The total estimated cost is $5,400, of which $2,000 is a revote.
Was there any vote for this last year? I do not see any amount in the revote column.

The reason it does not appear in the revote column is that the amount was voted in a previous year; it lapsed and it was not voted last year. We put this in to show the committee that there is a revote.
Cove Head-repairs to and strengthening shear dam, $1,250.
This is reported by the resident engineer to be necessary to prevent damage to the existing work.
Where is this?

It is in Queens county.
China Point-pier-renewals and repairs,

This is to make necessary repairs.
Haggerty's wharf-repairs to existing work and enlargement of pier head, $2,500.
This vote is asked for by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and the work is also reported as being necessary by the resident engineer.
Is this item sufficient to finish this work?

No; this will cost $4,000. We are asking for $2,500.
Harbours, rivers and bridges, generally- repairs and improvements, $10,000.

This is a general vote for all the different wharfs and bridges that are not specially provided for.
Lennox island and Port Hill - wharfs on Lennox Island Indian reserve and on main land opposite, near Port Hill; the Indian Department to contribute $2,500, $5,300.
This is to pay our portion of the construction of wharfs on the Indian reserve.
Is it customary for the Department of Public Works to construct wharfs and roads and make repairs on Indian reserve.

No, we do not build roads, but we do contribute very frequently, and I think as a general rule, towards the construction of wharfs where they are used by the public as well. Of course, if a wharf were regarded as one which would be absolutely private to the Indians, I presume that Our department would not contribute, but ordinarily we do contribute towards these wharfs.

My object in making the inquiry is that in my riding we have two large reserves and the people on either side of them are seriously in need of roads being opened up through them. If it were customary for the Department of Public Works to spend money on Indian reserves for roads and bridges it might be able to assist in this matter to which I have just called the attention of the minister.

The federal government does not build roads as a general thing, while it does build wharfs, as they are an aid to navigation.
Miminegash harbour-repairs, $2,500.
This is to repair and strengthen the works on either side of the channel entrance, also to extend the brush work and repair the approach.
How are the expenditures on these works going to be made?
By day's work.
I mean with reference to these votes generally.

If it is new work, even although it may be small, as a general rule, we ask for tenders, but if it is repair work, as a general rule, we do it by the day because it is impossible to tell what will be the extent of the repairs to an old wharf. You caimot tell until you begin to tear it away to see what the under timber is like, what the extent of the repairs will be, and it would be difficult, if not impossible, to let a contract for such work.
Naufrage pond - protecting entrance to channel with bridge across piers and roadways of approach, $4,000.

We require the $4,000 to complete it. There was an appropriation last year of $14,500 and it is probable that up to the 31st March next, there will be an expenditure of $11,000, leaving $3,500 which constitutes a revote; so that we are only asking $500 additional. The work is under contract.

Will this complete the
work?

Yes.
New London-repairs to breakwater, &c., $1,500.

This is to provide for repairs to the protection work on either side of the harbour entrance. These works are generally damaged by the fall and winter storms and the resident engineer reports that the work is needed.
Port Selkirk pier-repairs, $1,000.

This is to provide for the repairing and covering of the floor stringers of this pier, &c.
Mr. iPUGSLEY.
Red Point wharf-general repairs-revote of $1,500 lapsed, $1,000.
One thousand dollars will be necessary for this work.
How much is in that vote? There is a revote of $1,500 and there is only $1,000 now voted, what do you mean by that?
The session before last we had a vote of^ $1,500, none of which was used and we are now asking for $1,000.
Then it cannot be a revote of $1,500.

No, that is perhaps rather erroneous but all that means is that the total amount has lapsed. The object is to show the committee that it was once voted and not used.
Rustico breakwater-protection block at outer end, $6,000.
This is to provide for the extension of the present block at the outer end of the breakwater on the northern side of the entrance to the harbour.
What are these blocks made of ?

Timber, plank covering, cross-ties and ballast, bolts, close piling,
&c.
Are the stones cemented together or will they be loose?
Loose.
Has this breakwater been broken away by storms to any extent?
No, I think not. The extension is necessary to prevent the forming of a channel which would otherwise be formed. It is to change the direction of the current so as to preserve the navigable channel.
Will this finish the work?
Yes.
Will it be done by tender and contract?

Yes.
Souris-rip-rap protection on seaward side of Knight's Point breakwater and renewals and repairs-revote of $5,800 lapsed, $7,500.
Will this finish the work?
So it is estimated.

The hon. member for Kings (Mr. Fraser) has something to say with regard to some of these items and more particularly, I think, with the item under consideration. The hon. gentleman is unavoidably absent at the present moment, and I would ask the minister before

the items for Prince Edward Island are passed to allow one item to stand so that my hon. friend may have an opportunity for discussion.

I hope my hon. friend will not press to have the item stand, hut I will undertake that if the hon. member for Kings desires to speak on any item for Prince Edward Island, he can do so when any item for Quebec or Ontario is called, or, upon the dredging vote, or any convenient opportunity.
Or the supplementaries?
Yes.

That understanding is perfectly satisfactory.
Summerside harbour-for completion, &c., of breakwater extending from Indian Head to outer end of Lighthouse Spit, $10,000.
This is to complete the work which is under contract.
What is the 'total amount of the contract?

How long is this breakwater?	.	[DOT]
' Mr. PUGSLEY. 3,240 feet.
Is it merely a breakwater?

It is to afford protection to vessels lying at the wharf in the harbour during westerly and southerly gales.
Tignish-extension of harbour channel protection piers inwardly, $25,000.
The estimated cost including superintendence is $25,000, and we are asking for the full amount.
Is this contract work?

Yes.
Harbours and rivers, New Brunswick-Bay-side wharf on Johnston Cove, $1,500.
This is for a new wharf on the St. Croix river which will accommodate quite a number of farmers.
What is the total cost?
$1,500. It is expected this will cover the whole expenditure.
A portion of the cost of this wharf is not paid by the provincial government?

No.	'
Buctouche-channel through beach, inclusive of breastwork and breakwater repairs, $3,500.
What was the expenditure on this last year?
To the 31st September, $2,169.
When did the work beJ gin?
What is the total expenditure to date?
The total expenditure on harbour improvements at Buctouche has been $39,123, but I cannot say over what period that extends.
What is the object of this work?

The object of the cut through the beach was to effect a saving of ten or twelve miles in the sailing distance of the Buctouche fishing boats on their way to the fishing grounds, and the same distance is saved in the towing of logs. It also forms an entrance into a convenient harbour of refuge.
What is the length of the channel?
The length of one of the breakwaters is 2,800 feet.
What is the width of the channel?
It3 width is fifty feet. I cannot give my hon. friend its length.
Will this appropriation complete the channel?

It is expected that this will complete it. I should correct the statement which I made. The $39,123.75 which I mentioned was the total expenditure on Buctouche harbour works up to the 31st March, 1909. The total cost of this work to that date was $16,933.66.
Is there to be any dredging in connection with it?
Yes, 1,000 cubic yards.
Who does the dredging?
It is hand-dredging, done by a mud digger,, operated by a steam winch.
What is the depth of water?
Three feet at low water, and I am told about thirteen feet at high water.
My information is that the money that has been expended on this so-called public work is an absolute waste.
For what reason?

I will state it. The minister has stated that this work was begun in 1904, and that the object of it was to cut a channel so as to make a short cut for vessels going into Buctouche harbour. This expenditure has been going on year



after year since that time. There was expended in 1904 $2,438.93, in 1905 $1,895.17, in 1906 $5,960, in 1907 $1,998.92, in 1908 $3,500, in 1909, $3,773.75, a total of $19,556,27, and the amount asked for this year is $3,500. My information is that the work of one year is washed away in the following year and has to be completely renewed, and this has been going on during the past six or 3even years. When we look into the accounts for this work, we find that Mr. J. D. Irving, who was a witness in an investigation before the Public Accounts Committee the other day, has figured very largely in the money that has been appropriated for carrying on this work. I find that he has got out of it in these years $5,049, and that his brother, Mr. R. A. Irving has got out of it $1,538, or a total of $6,587, out of an expenditure of $19,556.27, a large proportion of which sum was for the rent of an engine and a scow.
How much for the rent of the engine and scow?

Mr. Irving, for a little bit of a scow, which he told us had cost him $150, and which he has owned for several years, has got from this government $514 as rent; he has been receiving $2 a day for it while this work has been going on during all these years. For an engine which he valued at $500 he has received $8 a day, or a total of $1,778.
Does not that $8 a day include the fuel and the hauling of fresh water for the engine and the wages of a man?

I understand that the claim is that it includes fuel and the wages of an engineer; but my information is that the man who runs the engine figures in the pay-roll. I do not say that absolutely, but that is the information I have. It seems to me that $19,556 expended in that way year after year is making a perfect farce of the expenditure of public money, If the work served any good purpose, there might not be quite so much ground of complaint; but I have it from reliable residents of that county that the work done two or three years ago was washed away and had to be done the following year and so on from year to year. It consists in getting a lot of brush and stone, for which Mr. J. D. Irving is paid $2.50 per cubic yard for large stone and $1 for small stone. Then his brother, who is a lawyer, has been supplying large quantities of stone also.
His brother does a very large general business outside of being a lawyer. He owns a mill, I think.

I think J. D. Irving owns the mill. It is a most extraordinary thing to find barristers of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick supplying stone Mr. CROCKET.
for public works, particularly at such prices. I do not think my hon. friend knows many reputable members of the legal profession in the province of New Brunswick who go into that kind of business. If you go into these accounts, you find that this money is being circulated largely among the Liberal managers of Kent county. The belief down there is that these appropriations year after year are made not so much in the public interest as to circulate the money among political friends of the government. Perhaps the minister can state exactly what condition this work is in. It has been of no service up to the present time; not a single boat has used the channel since it was started seven years ago. If the minister can assure us that this $3,509 will be the end of this expenditure, perhaps we will not have very such more to say. I do protest, however, against money being expended in such a perfectly useless work as this and expended in that wasteful manner. It seems to me that a work going on regularly year after year, consisting largely of what is spoken of as dredging done with a shovel-
It is not an ordinary hand shovel. It is a mud digger of the kind used on the north shore for digging mussel mud and is operated by a steam winch.
Who owns the mud digger?
I do not know.
Is it the property of the government or is rent paid for it?

It was not used very long, and I understood there was some work done with scrapers. My information is that this work will be effective for the purpose for which it is intended. The member for the county of Kent (Mr. LeBlanc) in whose judgment I have a very great deal of confidence, has represented to me that the work is of very great importance, and that when completed it will be effective for the purpose. One difficulty has been that instead of taking the whole amount required at once, so .as to complete the work in a short period it has been carried on from year to year. I shall look into the allegations of my hon. friend and see exactly the condition in which the work is, but my information has been that the work will be effective and that this $3,500 will complete it.
With regard to the moneys that have been paid to the Messrs. Irving my hon. friend should not take too seriously the suggestions or insinuations made by political opponents. There is a general disposition-among many people who are opposed to the government to create an impression that moneys are being wasted by being

paid overto political friends. I suppose that will be the case with all governments, Liberal or Conservative. My information is that the Messrs. Irving are thoroughly reliable people. It is not a crime that they happen to be Liberals, they are just as good men as if they were Tories, and the mere fact that they are Liberals ought not to imply that they have been paid more for the stone, or the engine, or the scow than their services were worth. It was proved before the committee that the engine was used for only a short period each year and that the charge of $8 a day was a reasonable charge and included, in addition to the hire of the engine, the fuel, the labour and expenditure of hauling fresh water a considerable distance for use in the engine and also labour of the men, so that the charge of $8 a day was reasonable. With regard to the scow, it was proved to be a large scow, well adapted for the purpose. It was used by the government for only a short period each year and during the past season, instead of renting it to the government, Mr. Irving was asked to rent it to a private contractor and it has been used during the past year at Cape Bald in the county of Westmorland, where he receives from a private contractor more than he was getting from the government. Therefore I do not take too seriously the suggestions of my hon. friend because I realize that when he makes them he is not speaking from his own knowledge but from statements made to him by others.

I am not condemning Mr. Irving because he is a Liberal. I would not condemn any man because he is a Liberal or a Conservative. I am condemning the department. My opinion and the opinions of those who have stated their opinions is not based upon the party affiliation of the Irvings at all. So far as I am concerned, it is based on the bald facts that appear by the Auditor General's Report and the value that Mr. Irving himself before the committee stated as the value of the scow and of the engine. My hon. friend states it was only used for' a few days of each year. In 1909 alone, he was paid for seventy-three days, or $584-
"Mr. PUGSLEY. That is only a little over two months.

-an amount consider-ablv in excess of the whole value of the engine. For the scow he was paid for 95 days at $2 a day, and the scow was worth $150. I do not, however, speak so much of that as of the perfect uselessness of this work. I ask the minister if he does not himself think it very strange that a small work of this character, the cutting of a short channel through a
mud flat to make a short cut into Buc-touche Harbour has been in progress year after year from 1904, with no more evidence of its being completed to-day than at the time the work was begun.

My hon. friend is aware that this is tidal water, and it is not so easy to make and complete and make perfect against storms a channel which is in tidal water, you have to protect it thoroughly with brush and stone.
And the reason is that the work which is done one year is as regularly washed away and must be renewed the next year.
I think my hon. friend is wrong. My information is right to the contrary.

The minister has no statement to make as to the necessity of this work. He has not shown that any boat or vessel has used this channel. It is not in a position to be used, notwithstanding the work has been going on for seven years, and all that time it has been carried on under this system of day labour and the purchase of stone from political friends in the neighbourhood.
What is the objection to the purchase of stone?
It has been purchased at $2.50 a yard.
These are very large stones.

I know one of the contractors at Riehibucto told me that some stone was bought from him at 5 cents a cubic yard. The minister should look into this matter and be able, before asking another appropriation, at least to state just what position the work is in, whether it is ever to be completed or if it is going to continue from year to year as in the past.

Before the Committee of Public Accounts, Mr. Irving swore posi lively that out of the supply of stone during the past year, after paying for quarrying and hauling the stone a considerable distance, his total profits were $36.
Did he quarry the stones?

Yes, and it is very desirable in work of this character, exposed to the action of the sea and storms and heavy winds, that the stone should be as large as possible. These stones for which $2.50 is charged, as my hon. friend says-I have not a memorandum of the charge before me -were very large stones, and for those of smaller size the charge was $1. There is evidence that out of the total year's supply, after paying expenses, of quarrying and

hauling the stone this considerable distance, the profits were only $36, which, I think, no one would call unreasonable.
Mr. Irving's statement applies to the first year, but I think he has gone on supplying stone since that time. Who was the conductor appointed for this work?
There was a foreman, sometimes called a conductor.
Has the minister his name?
Yes, Mr. A. Cormier.
Is the mud-digger there worked by hand or by this engine?

The mud-digger in use was worked by an engine. My information is that it was not used very much. I think the work has been done with scrapers at low tide. Still as to that I may be wrong.
Campbellton-deep water wharf, $5,000.
That is for completing the work.
Is the work under contract?
Yes.
Does this amount complete the work?
It is expected to complete the work.
What wharfage will this give?
It is 304 feet long by 35 feet wide. This is connected with the easterly end of the present wharf by a span of 15 feet.
Is that the extension?
Yes.
What will that make the total length of the deep water wharf?
The Shives wharf would be 250 feet in length. And, as well as I can make out, this would be added, making a total of 554 feet.
What depth of water have they there?
I think it is eighteen or twenty feet. Some dredging has been done.
Is that independent of the present contract?
Yes.
How much has been paid up to date?
To 30th of September last, the amount paid was $30,745.80.
What is the total amount of the contract?
The minister must be mistaken as to the amount paid, for in the last Auditor General's Report it appears that over $18,000 was paid.

Who is the contractor? Mr. William Glover. Of Campbellton?
Yes.
Cape Bald-breakwater pier, $18,500.
This is to build a breakwater and wharf at Cape Bald in the county of Westmorland, and is to make provision for the completion of the contract.
What is the total cost?

The amount of the contract is $32,890, to which there is to be added superintendence, contingencies, &c., $3,110, and also the cost of making a road $2,729.36. The total estimated cost is $38,729.36. This is being built of concrete. It is in a place where the work will be much exposed to storms and where it is very desirable to have a work of a permanent character.
Was this a new contract in the year ending March 31, 1909?
Tenders were called for in the fall of 1908 and the contract was let in the spring of 1909.
How many tenders were received?
Four, and the contract was, as usual, given to the lowest.
To whom?
Mr. E. A. Wallberg.
Did the minister or the department have representations as to the necessity of the work?
Yes.
From whom?

Among others, from the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Em-merson). I think there were also representations from the farmers and fishermen. This is an important place in the county of Westmorland, and is situated between Shediae and Cape Tormentine. It is quite distant from the railway, and the people who raise large quantities of farm produce,

have had no means of shipping, and so were at a great disadvantage. It will be a great advantage to them to be afforded the means which this wharf will give them of shipping the prodfuce either to Cape Tor-mentine or to Shediac..
Was there no wharf there before?
None.

Why did the department decide to make it of concrete?
Mr. PUGSLEY, First, because it is in an exposed place. Concrete is rapidly becoming a favourite material for the construction of wharfs as well as buildings. Besides, this is in a locality where, as was represented to us, I believe, the .teredo was likely to do considerable damage to a wooden wharf. Taking all these things together, we thought it would be better to build a concrete wharf.
Has the department built other concrete wharfs in New Brunswick?

I do not know as to New Brunswick. We have built them on the Ottawa river. There is one at Arn-prior. We have just completed one also at -Lakefield, a very fine wharf. It was not found to foe much more expensive than timber.

Was this contract let in bulk sum?
Cape Tormentine-breakwater, $5,000.
This is to rebuild the facing and replace the stone. It is asked for by the resident engineer. It was built many years ago, and requires annual repairs.
I see on V-182 that the department bought an old flat car from the Intercolonial railway for $150. What was that for?

In 1908-9 the sum of $9,226 was expended in driving 74 creosoted piles along the pier head. Ballasting and covering the pier head was completed for about 2,200 square feet. A flat car was purchased from the Intercolonial on which to erect a derrick. This was used in handling and placing 823 cubic yards of large stone, to raise the slope alongside the face of the pier head.

I would call attention to the fact that the stone that was obtained for this breakwater was paid at the Tate of $3.50 per cubic yard, whereas that used at Buctouche was paid for at the rate of $2.50. The money is being paid to Mr. H. C. Reid, I do not know if he is a lawyer.
I think Mr. Reid is proprietor of the Stone Quarries at or near Sackville.
Is this work being done by contract, or by day labour?
By day labour.
It was a bulk sum contract.
Who were the other tenderers?
I cannot give the names. Four tenders were received, ranging from $32,890 to $62,000. The lowest was accepted.
It did not occur to the department to rent that car from the Intercolonial.

We got it at a very reasonable price.
Chance harbour-to raise inclined low tide landing pier up to high water level, $2,800.
Does the government acquire the title to the land?
We acquired the title on the 6th of October, 1908, for the sum of $310. It consists of six and a half acres.

The present pier is 176 feet long, 25 feet wide and 18 feet high at the outer end, but it is covered at high tide, and this is to raise it up. It means the general elevation of the whole breakwater about 8 feet.
The minister spoke about the right of way to the wharf costing $3,000.

That would be for building the approach. This $310 would include the right of way and the site for the breakwater. The roadway was done by day labour, and is completed. That expenditure was made in 1908-9.
Most of it in October, I suppose?
No, it Tan over eight months. We got through with it on the 30th of November.
Will this cover the whole expense?

This will cover the whole cost.
Cummings Cove, Deer island-wharf, $15,000.

This is to make provision towards the construction of a wharf at Cummings Cove. It is for the building of a trestle approach 23 feet wide and 290 feet in length, consisting of pile work. The total estimated cost will be $19,400, outside of superintendence.
Was there anything spent on this last year?

No, we called for tenders but the tenders submitted were considerably higher than the engineer's estimate, we declined to award the contract and propose to call for new tenders.
Dalhousie harbour-breakwater, $10,000.

This is to build a breakwater at Dalhousie to protect the basin. There was a sort of breakwater there which had been built up with mill refuse and edgings, and that sort of thing, and it had been used as a roadway. The central part of that has been washed away and this has exposed the inner harbour, sometimes called the Ferry Harbour, to the storms. It will be very inconvenient, if not somewhat dangerous, for vessels unless this breakwater is built. It will be very useful, as it will give protection to the harbour.
This is called the Ferry wharf?
No, not this breakwater. This leads from a point out to the island, and it is to be a new work.
Is this to replace the old breakwater the minister spoke of as being composed of mill reluse?
This will replace it.
By whom is that property owned?

It will belong to the public. The title will be in the Crown. It was under the control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. But, of course, that will be looked into carefully to see that the title is in the Crown. The Department of Marine, I believe, own the island. They have taken it under expropriation. I think this would be the foreshore extending out from the shore of the river to the island, but, of course, we will look into that carefully before expending the money.
When did the Department of Marine and Fisheries acquire the island?
Perhaps about a year ago.
And the intention of this work is to connect that island with the mainland?
Yes, it will extend from the shore to Douglas island.
That extends from the property of the Dalhousie Lumber Company to Moffatt's Island, which has been purchased by the government?
No, I think the property of the Dalhousie Lumber Company would be rather to the westward of this
breakwater. I do not think they own from the point at which this breakwater will proceed. Douglas Island was expropriated by the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Does the minister know how much the island cost the Marine Department?
I do not, but I understand the amount was not large.

The reason I ask the minister about this is that there is an impression that a large amount of the work that has been done by the Department of Public Works at Dalhousie has been for the benefit of the Dalhousie Lumber Company.
Mr.	PUGSLEY.	Who	entertains	that
impression?

That is the general impression prevalent at Dalhousie.
Mr.	PUGSLEY.	That	surprises	me
greatly.

Most of the dredging which was done at Dalhousie last year was done along the wharf frontage of the Dalhousie Lumber	Company. I wa3 informed that the Minister of Public Works is a stock holder of the Dalhousie Lumber Company. Perhaps the minister will deny that?
Mr.	PUGSLEY.	Why	does the	hon.
gentleman think that the minister would deny it?
Does the minister deny it?
He does .not.

There is no question about the fact that A. and R. Loggie have been paid thousands of dollars for dredging for the benefit of the Dalhousie Lumber Oompany. I was at Dalhousie last summer myself and saw the Loggie dredge at work dredging out and making more valuable the property of the Dalhousie Lumber Company, and that work is being paid for, although it is entirely for the benefit of the Dalhousie Lumber Company, out of the public treasury. It is a matter that members of this House have a right to protest against. There is no doubt that much of this same thing has been going on all over the country. Item after item, involving thousands of dollars, is being asked and appropriated by this parliament year after year for the building up of private property. That is a fact in reference to the work at Dalhousie. It is true that the minister has spoken of the basin at Dalhousie that lies beyond the lines of the company's property but the major part of the dredging which was done last year was done right at the wharf of the Dalhousie Lumber Company. Perhaos when

the dredging items come up we can get some further information in reference to this matter, and discuss it more fully. I do not think that this House should be asked year after year to appropriate large sums for the benefit of private corporations. There are hundreds of places throughout this country where public money is being spent in this way while hundreds of other communities are crying out in vain for appropriations which are urgently required in the public interest.
I think it would be much more convenient if the hon. gentleman would discuss the item before the committee. When the dredging vote comes up he will be able to discuss this matter.

I mention that in connection with the information the minister has already communicated to the committee that the appropriation which is now being asked is for the purpose of removing that old breakwater, as he terms it. In fact it is nothing more than a bridge which was for the convenience of the Moffat firm, from whom the Dalhousie Lumber Company acquired their property, and the work now proposed includes the replacement of the roadway of which he speaks. I have understood that it is a work in the interest of the Dalhousie Lumber Company, whose propery lies right at that point. That is the reason why I have said what I have in reference to the dredging, because when we have this vote in reference to the dredging and another large expenditure for this so called breakwater which is lying at the same point, it appears to add colour at least to the belief that public money is being appropriated in the interest of a lumber company of which the minister is a stockholder.

My hon. friend is entirely in error in so far as this work is concerned. This work is to protect what is known as the Ferry harbour. There is a public wharf, the ferry runs there, there is a large traffic and this is for the erection of a public breakwater. In so far as it being a benefit to the Dalhousie Lumber Company is concerned I am not aware that it will be of special benefit to them, although, by reason of their owning one or two of the large mills at Dalhousie carrying on a very large lumber business, the largest lumber business there, and in view of the shipping constantly resorting to the port for the purpose of carrying away the lumber which they manufacture, I suppose, to a certain extent, they will derive a benefit from it. The Dalhousie Lumber Company will get the same benefit as any other firm carrying on business in the town. So far as I am aware this is not to be built on the property of the Dalhousie Lumber Company at all and the object of it is to protect
and improve the basin which is a public harbour. The hon. gentleman has asked me if I am a stockholder in the Dalhousie Lumber Company. It is true that some six or seven years ago I took some stock in that company. I paid my money for the stock the same as other people did and I can assure the hon. gentleman there was no watered stock' in connection with that company; every _ man paid his hard cash. That company is engaged in large lumbering operations upon the Restigouche river and its vicinity cutting some 25,000,000 feet per year. I happen to be one of the stockholders.
Will this involve the purchase of any property from the Dalhousie Lumber Company, or any rights?
None whatever so far as I am aware.
